issues.description:
Archive the raw fetched bytes for every accepted reference, not just PDFs. This is link-rot insurance, and it is the precondition for scaling ingestion safely.

## Why this is high priority

Ingestion has been deliberately throttled out of a fear of importing references that would need re-importing if the knowledge-base architecture changed. That fear is mostly unfounded — and understanding exactly why identifies the one place it IS founded.

**What is already safely re-derivable** (no re-import needed, ever): chunking strategy, embedding model, distillation artifacts, entity extraction, entity resolution, contextual prefixes, index rebuilds. All of these re-derive from stored `extracted_text` attachments plus the GraphQL records. The vector index is explicitly derived state.

**What is NOT re-derivable**: anything that requires the original fetched artifact. If we later want tables, figures, layout, embedded images, or simply better extraction than today's extractor produced, we must re-fetch — and by then the source may be gone, edited, or paywalled. Threat-intelligence sources are unusually prone to this: vendors pull advisories, revise them silently, and move reports behind registration.

So the durable asset is the raw bytes. Everything else is a projection of them.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-25)

The machinery already exists and is well built — it is simply gated too narrowly.

- `_reference_source_attachment_record` (`src/papyrus_content/reference_url_text.py:3378`) creates a `role="source"` attachment holding raw `content: bytes`, with a sha256 of the body, a `filename` derived from URI + media type, and a storage path under `{corpus_prefix}/source/{reference_folder}/{filename}` (falling back to `corpora/reference-source/...`). `sortKey` is `001-source`.
- It has exactly two call sites, and **both are gated on the source being a PDF**:
  - `reference_url_text.py:166` — `if _looks_like_pdf_uri(extraction_source_uri):`
  - `reference_url_text.py:257` — `if is_pdf_source:` (also inside `if allow_discovery:`)
- Consequence: an accepted HTML reference stores extracted text but **no archival copy of the page**. For this publication that is the majority of the corpus.
- `_download_source_attachment_from_uri(uri, reference=...)` already exists and does the fetching.

## Design decisions

1. **Archive raw bytes for every accepted reference regardless of media type.** Remove the PDF gating; keep the same `role="source"` attachment shape, storage layout, and sha256 so nothing downstream changes. For HTML, store the response body as fetched (do not pretty-print, do not rewrite).
2. **Archive at accession, not at proposal.** Only accepted references get archived — this preserves the curation gate as the cost governor and avoids storing bytes for rejected prospects. (Consider as a follow-up whether high-value pending prospects deserve a provisional snapshot, given that the accept decision may come days after discovery and the page may change in between. Note it; do not build it here.)
3. **Record fetch provenance in the attachment metadata**: `downloadedAt`, final URL after redirects, HTTP status, `contentType`, and content length, alongside the existing `source`/`sourcePlugin` fields. Provenance is what makes an archive trustworthy later.
4. **Idempotency by content hash.** The record already computes a sha256. Skip the re-upload when an existing `source` attachment has a matching hash; when it differs, that is a *signal* — the source changed after we captured it. Log it and consider retaining both (see 5).
5. **Never overwrite an existing archived body silently.** Either keep the first capture or version the captures. Silent overwrite would destroy the exact evidence this epic exists to preserve.
6. **Size guard.** Cap archived bodies (suggest a few MB) with the limit configurable; log and skip oversize responses rather than failing accession. S3 is cheap but unbounded downloads are not.
7. **Backfill is part of this epic.** A CLI operation that walks already-accepted non-PDF references and archives what is still reachable, reporting what is already gone. That report is itself valuable: it quantifies how much has already been lost.

## Files to modify

- `src/papyrus_content/reference_url_text.py` — remove PDF gating at both call sites; extend metadata; hash-based idempotency; size guard.
- CLI wiring (`src/papyrus_newsroom/references_commands.py` or sibling) — a backfill command plus a coverage report ("N accepted references, M archived, K unreachable").
- Tests: HTML source archives bytes; PDF path unchanged; identical content does not re-upload; changed content is detected and reported; oversize is skipped not fatal; backfill reports unreachable sources.

## What could go wrong

- **Cost**: raw bytes are larger than extracted text, but this is S3 at hobby-project scale — pennies. Verify with the backfill report's total-bytes figure rather than assuming.
- **Fetching at accession may hit paywalls or bot protection** that the original discovery fetch got past, so archival can fail where extraction succeeded. Record the failure on the reference rather than silently skipping; a reference with no archive is a known-fragile citation.
- **Legal/ethical**: archiving full copies for internal evidentiary use is ordinary practice, but the archive must never be republished. Keep it internal-only; it is provenance, not content.
- **Do not let this block accession.** Archival failure should degrade to a warning, never reject an accepted reference.
- **The backfill will find losses.** Expect some already-accepted sources to be unreachable. That is the cost of having waited, and it is an argument for landing this before ingestion ramps, not after.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every newly accepted reference of any media type has a `role="source"` attachment with raw bytes and a content hash.
- Backfill run and its coverage report recorded, including how many sources were already unrecoverable.
- Re-running accession on unchanged content performs no redundant upload.
issues.title: Archive raw source bytes for all accepted references (link-rot insurance)

issues.description:
Build a golden-query evaluation harness and capture a BASELINE before any retrieval-changing epic lands. This is the highest-leverage epic on the board despite being the least glamorous: without it we can ship six retrieval changes and be unable to distinguish "improved," "no change," and "made it worse."

DO THIS FIRST. Its baseline numbers are an acceptance criterion for every other retrieval epic.

## Why this exists

Cerebras had 15,000 queries/day of real users telling them what was broken — their lessons were legible because they had a feedback loop. We have a handful of agent-driven queries and no measurement at all. Rank fusion genuinely CAN make retrieval worse: a lexical arm that confidently ranks weak matches on natural-language queries dilutes previously-decent semantic results. Two retrievers with untuned weights are not automatically better than one. We need to be able to tell.

## Design decisions (current thinking — challenge them if you have better information)

1. **Golden set: ~25 queries built from the ACTUAL accepted corpus**, not synthetic fixtures. Procedure: list accepted references (`references export-analysis-manifest` or GraphQL listing), read a sample, write queries whose correct answers you can verify by hand. Store as `procedures/newsroom/tests/fixtures/retrieval_golden_queries.json`: `[{id, query, expect_reference_lineage_ids: [...], category, notes}]`.
2. **Required coverage categories** (roughly equal counts):
   - `identifier` — exact CVE IDs, hashes, domains, ATT&CK IDs appearing verbatim in a known reference. THESE ARE EXPECTED TO FAIL at baseline; that failure is the business case for the hybrid-lexical epic.
   - `paraphrase` — question vocabulary deliberately disjoint from the source's vocabulary.
   - `freshness` — two references answering the same question, different ages; expectation is the newer one ranks first.
   - `quality_tie` — comparable relevance, different quality ratings.
   - `multi_hop` — answer requires chaining two references (baseline for future graph work).
3. **Metrics**: hit@5, hit@10, MRR, plus per-category breakdown. Per-category matters more than the aggregate — a change that improves paraphrase while destroying identifier lookup must be visible, and the aggregate would hide it.
4. **Runner**: a CLI subcommand or pytest-marked-slow test that executes the golden set against `run_knowledge_query` locally (`--execution local`) and writes a timestamped JSON report to `procedures/newsroom/tests/fixtures/reports/`. Must run without deployed infrastructure beyond the vector index and GraphQL read access.
5. **Adversarial-authorship guard**: the same mind writing the eval and the features will unconsciously write queries the system already handles. Explicitly include queries you EXPECT to fail today. If the baseline scores near-perfect, the golden set is wrong — rewrite it harder.
6. **No LLM judging in v1.** Expected-reference-ID matching only. Deterministic, free, and sufficient for ranking comparisons.

## Files

- NEW `procedures/newsroom/tests/fixtures/retrieval_golden_queries.json`
- NEW runner (module + CLI wiring or marked test — implementer's choice, document it)
- Baseline report committed to the repo so future diffs are reviewable.

## What could go wrong

- **Golden set too easy** → every epic "passes" and we learn nothing. See decision 5; the identifier category should be visibly broken at baseline.
- **Corpus drift** invalidates expected IDs as references are superseded (versioned lineage!). Pin expectations to `lineageId`, NOT `id`, and have the runner report unresolvable expectations as errors rather than misses.
- **Overfitting to 25 queries.** Treat the set as a regression guard, not proof of general improvement. Grow it whenever a real retrieval failure is observed in practice — that is the highest-value source of new cases.
- **Baseline captured after epic 1 lands** would make the whole thing pointless. Capture and commit the baseline BEFORE any retrieval-changing merge.

## Acceptance criteria

- Baseline report committed, with identifier-category scores visibly poor (documenting the gap the roadmap exists to close).
- Runner reproducible by a second person from the README/docstring alone.
- Every subsequent retrieval epic can produce a before/after table from this harness.
issues.title: Retrieval eval harness: golden queries + baseline

issues.description:
Add exact-token (BM25) retrieval alongside vector search and fuse the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion. This is the anchor investment: today a query for `CVE-2024-3400` or a file hash is served purely by embedding similarity, which blurs exact strings. Three other epics stack on this one.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-19)

- Retrieval is vector-only: `S3VectorsProvider.search` (`src/papyrus_knowledge_query/services.py:306+`), called from `run_knowledge_query` (`engine.py:194-207`). On failure it warns and continues (`engine.py:205-206`) — mirror that degradation pattern.
- The only "lexical" code is `lexical_relevance` (`ranking.py:225-233`), a metadata-overlap fallback used when a record has no score/distance. Not an index.
- Provider protocol: `SemanticSearchProvider` with `search(query, scope, limit)` (`services.py:185-189`). The lexical provider must implement this and return the SAME match-record shape as `S3VectorsProvider` (inspect its return value and what `_normalize_semantic_matches` at `engine.py:209` expects — keys like key/score/metadata).
- Chunk identity: `_prepare_chunks` (`vector_index.py:720-756`) keys passage vectors as `reference-passage-<sha256(lineageId:storagePath:chunkIndex)[:20]>`. The lexical index MUST use the same keys so lexical hits join/dedupe with vector hits.
- Sync pipeline to piggyback on: `index_reference_passages` (`vector_index.py:91+`) already lists accepted references, reads extracted text, and chunks it, with audit/sync/rebuild actions.
- Lambda env already has `PAPYRUS_STORAGE_BUCKET_NAME` (`amplify/backend.ts:609`). Its S3 read grant covers ONLY the `corpora/*` prefix (`grantCorporaRead`, `backend.ts:324-331,376`).
- Thread-safe lazy boto3 client pattern to copy: `S3CorpusTextProvider` (`services.py:268+`).

## Design decisions (current thinking — challenge them if you have better information)

1. **Pure-Python BM25 inverted index, gzipped JSON artifact in S3.** No new services, no pip dependencies (Lambda is stdlib-only). OpenSearch is disqualified (cost floor × N instances); SQLite FTS5 rejected (runtime compile-flag gamble); DynamoDB inverted index rejected (write amplification, more failure modes).
2. **Artifact key: `corpora/knowledge-index/lexical/v1/index.json.gz`** — deliberately under `corpora/` to reuse the existing Lambda read grant with ZERO backend.ts changes. The build side (CLI sync) writes with local AWS credentials, so no write grant needed on the Lambda.
3. **Artifact contents**: `{version: 1, builtAt, k1: 1.2, b: 0.75, avgdl, docs: [{key, referenceLineageId, chunkIndex, corpusId, curationStatus, title}], df: {term: docCount}, postings: {term: [[docIdx, tf], ...]}}`. Docs are chunk-level, keyed identically to passage vectors.
4. **Threat-intel tokenizer** (new function in the new module — do NOT modify `keyword_set` or `_keywords`): preserve as atomic terms CVE IDs (`CVE-\d{4}-\d{4,7}`), hex hashes (`[a-fA-F0-9]{32,64}`), ATT&CK IDs (`T\d{4}(\.\d{3})?`), domains, IPs. Normalize defanged IOCs BEFORE tokenizing, at both index time and query time: `hxxp`→`http`, `[.]`→`.`, `(.)`→`.`, `[at]`→`@`. Lowercase everything else; min token length 3; reuse a stopword set.
5. **New module `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/lexical_index.py`**: builder (`build_lexical_index(...)` called from `index_reference_passages`), serializer, and `BM25LexicalProvider` (loads artifact from S3 lazily into a module-level cached global; also accepts a local file path for tests/local CLI). Ships to the Lambda automatically because bundling copies the whole package.
6. **Fusion: new `fuse_ranked_lists(lists, *, weights=None, k=60)` in `ranking.py`** implementing RRF: `score(d) = Σ weight_l / (k + rank_l(d))`, joined on record key. Normalize the fused score to 0..1 (divide by the theoretical max `Σ weight_l / (k + 1)`) and feed it through the existing `relevance` component so quality/graphContext weighting still applies (`relevance_score_from_record`, `ranking.py:210-222` — fused records should carry the normalized value in `score`).
7. **Call site**: in `run_knowledge_query` around `engine.py:194-207`, run semantic and lexical searches in parallel threads (`concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`; the embedding HTTP call dominates latency), fuse, then pass the fused list into `_normalize_semantic_matches` unchanged. Record provenance on each match: `fusion: {semanticRank, lexicalRank, rrfScore}` — needed for debugging and the future rerank epic.
8. **Identifier-query boost**: if the query matches the CVE/hash/ATT&CK/domain regexes, set the lexical list weight to 1.5 (default 1.0). An exact-identifier query should strongly favor exact matches.
9. **Graceful degradation**: missing/unparseable artifact → append a warning and continue semantic-only (exactly like the existing semantic-failure handling). Never hard-fail a query because the lexical artifact is absent.

## Files to modify

- NEW `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/lexical_index.py` — tokenizer, builder, serializer, `BM25LexicalProvider`.
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/vector_index.py` — call the builder inside `index_reference_passages` (same pass over the same chunks); include the artifact in `audit` comparisons.
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/ranking.py` — add `fuse_ranked_lists`.
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/engine.py` — parallel search + fusion at the `engine.py:194-207` call site.
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/services.py` — construct the lexical provider alongside the semantic provider (mirror how `S3CorpusTextProvider` gets its bucket name); wire a local-path variant for `--execution local`.
- `procedures/newsroom/tests/test_knowledge_query.py` + new test module for the tokenizer/BM25/RRF.

## What could go wrong

- **Key mismatch between lexical docs and vector passages** silently breaks fusion joins and dedupe. Test explicitly: build both from the same fixture and assert key equality.
- **Scope filters**: `S3VectorsProvider` filters by corpusId/curationStatus etc. server-side. The lexical provider must apply the same scope filters post-scoring using the doc-table fields, or scoped queries will leak out-of-scope lexical hits. Write a test for corpus-scoped queries.
- **Staleness**: a reference rejected after the last sync stays in the lexical artifact until the next sync. This is the SAME staleness semantics as the vector index — accept it, but make `audit` report it.
- **Artifact size / cold start**: fine at current corpus size (tens of MB of text → a few MB gzipped). Add a size log line at build; if it ever exceeds ~50 MB inflated, revisit (SQLite fallback noted in the design doc).
- **Thread safety**: boto3 clients aren't thread-safe to CREATE concurrently; copy the `S3CorpusTextProvider` lock pattern. The OpenAI embedding call and the S3 GET run in separate threads — keep both failure paths independent (either can degrade alone).
- **Relevance-scale regression**: fused scores must stay in 0..1 or `relevance_score_from_record` will misinterpret them (it divides raw scores >1 by 25 — see `ranking.py:210-216`). Clamp and test.
- **Don't break `--execution local`**: the CLI local path has no S3; the provider must accept a local artifact path or degrade with a warning.

## Acceptance criteria

- A query containing a literal CVE ID returns the reference containing that string as a top result, even when embedding similarity alone would not surface it (fixture test).
- A defanged query (`hxxp://example[.]com`) matches a fanged occurrence and vice versa.
- Semantic-only behavior is byte-identical when the artifact is absent (plus one warning).
- `knowledge vector-index --action sync` builds/updates the artifact; `audit` reports artifact-vs-corpus drift.

## Out of scope

Rerank, contextual chunk prefixes, entity extraction (separate epics). The Epic "domain scoring cleanup" touches `_passage_score`/`_keywords` — coordinate if in flight simultaneously, but this epic must not modify those functions.
issues.title: Hybrid lexical (BM25) retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion

issues.description:
Add a recency signal to ranking so that when relevance and quality are otherwise equal, newer evidence wins. Threat-intel evidence rots fast; today a reference's age has zero influence, and publication dates aren't even stored in the vector index.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-19)

- `sourcePublishedAt`/`sourceUpdatedAt` are used only in display text. `_base_reference_metadata` (`src/papyrus_knowledge_query/vector_index.py:759-788`) writes NO date fields into vector metadata, even though the reference listing already fetches them.
- Ranking: `score_record` (`ranking.py:236-266`) blends relevance/quality/graphContext per `PROFILE_WEIGHTS` (`ranking.py:13-17`). Weights are normalized to sum 1.0 in `normalize_ranking_config` (`ranking.py:50-87`).
- The missing-value convention to copy: `missingQuality` defaults to 0.5 (`ranking.py:75-79`).
- CRITICAL PLUMBING DETAIL: `_normalize_semantic_matches` in `engine.py` copies a specific allowlist of metadata keys from vector matches onto normalized records (around `engine.py:1190-1202` — locate the copy list). New metadata keys are silently dropped unless added there. The same applies to passage ranking assignment (`_assign_passage_ranking`, around `engine.py:2214`).

## Design decisions (current thinking — challenge them if you have better information)

1. **Metadata**: add `sourcePublishedAtDay`, `sourceUpdatedAtDay`, `retrievedAtDay` as epoch-day INTEGERS (filterable; S3 Vectors filters need scalars) in `_base_reference_metadata`. Parse ISO-8601 including trailing `Z`; treat naive datetimes as UTC.
2. **Ranking**: add a `recency` component to `score_record` and all three `PROFILE_WEIGHTS` entries. Score: `0.5 ** (age_days / half_life)` with `half_life` configurable as `ranking.recencyHalfLifeDays`, default 180. Missing date → 0.5 (neutral, mirroring missingQuality). Clamp negative ages (future dates) to 0.
3. **Weight: small.** Default `recency: 0.07` taken proportionally from the existing weights before renormalization (balanced becomes ~0.65/0.23/0.05/0.07). Recency is a TIE-BREAKER — an authoritative two-year-old reference must still beat a thin fresh one. Do not exceed 0.10 in any default profile.
4. **Rank-side only.** No provider-side date filtering or decay (avoid double-counting). Use the freshest available date: max(sourceUpdatedAtDay, sourcePublishedAtDay).
5. `normalize_ranking_config` accepts `recencyHalfLifeDays` and a `recency` weight override, with the same validation/warning patterns as existing keys.

## Files to modify

- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/vector_index.py` — `_base_reference_metadata` date fields (verify the reference listing query already selects the date columns; it does per the audit, near the top of the file).
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/ranking.py` — `PROFILE_WEIGHTS`, `normalize_ranking_config`, `score_record`, plus a `recency_score(age_days, half_life)` helper.
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/engine.py` — add the new date keys to the metadata copy allowlist in `_normalize_semantic_matches` and thread them to `_assign_passage_ranking` / graph-resolved records (graph records can read dates from the reference row directly — full effect on vector matches needs the rebuild).
- `procedures/newsroom/tests/test_knowledge_query.py` — decay math unit tests; a two-otherwise-equal-records test where the newer wins; a missing-date-neutral test; a weights-renormalization test.

## What could go wrong

- **Existing score snapshots shift** because renormalization changes all weights slightly. Update expectations deliberately, not mechanically — verify orderings that should be stable stay stable.
- **The metadata allowlist.** If the new keys aren't added to `_normalize_semantic_matches`, the feature silently no-ops for vector matches (dates lost in normalization). Add a test that a synthetic vector match with a date metadata field produces a non-neutral recency score.
- **Rebuild required for full effect.** Vector metadata only updates on re-put. Do NOT trigger a solo rebuild for this — the change is backward-compatible (missing dates are neutral), so it can ride along with the next rebuild (the distillation/contextual-chunks epics batch one). State this in the PR description.
- **Timezone bugs**: use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`; never naive `now()`.

## Out of scope

Provider-side date range filters (nice-to-have; note as follow-up), any embedding changes, the rebuild itself.

issues.description:
Delete dead configuration surface and unvalidated tuning knobs from the retrieval layer. This is a subtraction-only change: no new behavior, less code, fewer constants. Do it early — it makes every later epic simpler, and it is the cheapest possible contractor calibration task.

## The finding that motivates this

**Nothing in the codebase ever sets `ranking.profile` or `ranking.diversity`.** There is no CLI flag for either, and no newsroom procedure passes them. Every knowledge query that has ever run used `balanced`/`balanced`. That is 3 ranking profiles + 3 diversity profiles — roughly 27 constants — of which exactly one path has ever executed. It reads as sophistication and functions as dead weight.

(Verify this before deleting: `grep -rn 'diversity\|"ranking"' src/papyrus_knowledge_query/cli.py src/papyrus_newsroom/tactus_runtime.py procedures/newsroom/*.tac`. The `diversity` hits in `src/papyrus_newsroom/coverage_theme.py` are a DIFFERENT concept — source diversity for coverage themes — and must not be touched.)

## Cuts, in order of value

1. **Delete `graphContext` as a weighted ranking signal.** `PROFILE_WEIGHTS` gives it 0.05 (`ranking.py:13-17`), meaning it can move a final score by at most 0.05 — noise, not signal. Deleting it removes the weight plus four hand-tuned constants in `_rank_structured_records` (`engine.py:2161-2180`: 1.0 for anchors, 0.9 for semantic-match-that-is-also-a-graph-neighbor, 0.6 for shares-context-metadata, 0.8 for expanded objects), and `_shares_context_metadata` may become dead code — check and remove if so.
   - This is consistent with AD-1, which makes graph a fused ranked list rather than a scalar nudge. If the hybrid-lexical/fusion epic has already landed, fold graph in as a third list at that time; if it has not, deleting the signal now is still correct, because a 0.05-weight nudge is not doing useful work either way. Renormalize the remaining weights.
   - Anchors currently get `graph_context=1.0` AND `relevance=1.0` — deleting the graph term must not change anchor behavior, since anchors are explicitly requested objects. Verify anchors still sort first.
2. **Collapse the three diversity profiles to one.** Keep the `balanced` values as plain constants; delete `focused` and `broad`, `VALID_DIVERSITY_PROFILES`, and the `diversity` config plumbing (`ranking.py:19-47`, and the `rankingDiversity` pass-through at `engine.py:198`). Restore them from git history if a real need ever appears.
3. **Delete the `reporting` consumer profile.** It is a near-duplicate of `reporter` (both depth 1, insightBias 1.0; topK 10 vs 12) and appears only in `VALID_PROFILES` (`engine.py:26`) and the CLI `choices` list (`cli.py:28`). Confirm no procedure or caller passes `profile="reporting"` before removing; if any does, point it at `reporter`.
4. **Consider collapsing the remaining consumer profiles.** `researcher`/`editor`/`reviewer` differ only in `insightBias` (1.25/1.15/1.35) and topK (18/20/20) — gradations nobody measured. Merging them into one research-depth profile is defensible. **Optional and reversible; use judgment, and if in doubt leave them.** Unlike cuts 1-3 this one removes a distinction someone may have intended.

## Why this is worth doing before the other epics

Every deleted constant is one fewer thing later work has to reason about, and cuts 1 and 2 remove tuning surface in exactly the code the fusion and recency epics will modify. Deleting first means those epics touch simpler code.

## What could go wrong

- **Existing tests may assert on removed profiles or on scores that shift after weight renormalization.** Run `pytest procedures/newsroom/tests/test_knowledge_query.py` first, understand every failure before changing an expectation, and confirm that result *orderings* which should be stable remain stable.
- **Renormalization changes every score slightly.** That is expected. If the retrieval eval harness exists, run it before and after: this change should be behavior-neutral in ranking order, and the harness is how you prove that rather than assert it.
- **Do not touch `coverage_theme.py`** — its `diversity` is unrelated.
- **Do not delete `quality`** — it is genuinely used, fed by `quality_rating_is` relations, and it is the signal that encodes editorial judgment.

## Acceptance criteria

- Net negative diff.
- No behavior change in result ordering for a set of representative queries (or eval-harness parity if it exists).
- No remaining references to deleted profiles anywhere, including CLI choices and docs.
issues.title: Delete dead ranking config and unvalidated tuning knobs

`procedures/newsroom/tests/test_references_commands.py` reports **10 failed, 54 passed**. These failures predate the link-rot archival work (`f2b9ed5`) — verified by running the same suite against `HEAD~1`, where the identical 10 fail. They are not a regression from that epic.

## Why this is worth its own issue

A red baseline is not cosmetic — it actively hides defects. All 10 failures are in `test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans*`, which are exactly the tests that exercise the function where the archival epic introduced an `UnboundLocalError` on `corpus_key`. The bug reached a closed issue partly because the tests that would have caught it were already failing and therefore being ignored.

Every epic in this initiative touches code covered by this suite. Until it is green, "tests pass" is not a signal anyone can act on, and each new change compounds the problem.

## Failing tests

```
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans_falls_back_to_raw_when_filter_fails
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans_passthrough_for_pdf_sources
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans_pdf_only_skips_non_pdf_sources
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans_records_grobid_metadata
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans_tracks_doi_resolution_counters
test_build_reference_url_text_attachment_plans_uses_enrichment_canonical_uri_and_reference_metadata
test_non_pdf_does_not_override_reference_source_published_at
test_pdf_grobid_publication_date_invalid_preserves_existing_reference_source_published_at
test_pdf_grobid_publication_date_overwrites_reference_source_published_at
```

Observed symptom in at least one case: `IndexError: list index out of range` at `test_references_commands.py:645`, which reads like the test expecting more entries in a plans/records list than the function now returns.

## Likely cause — investigate before fixing

Recent commits touching this area, newest first:

- `d079fa8` "Fix reference metadata round-trip on the lean TI schema" — modified `reference_url_text.py`, `records.py`, `model_attachments.py`.
- `8973fa3` "Trim SemanticNode query fields to match the deployed lean schema".

The "lean TI schema" work changed which fields and records are produced. The most probable story is that the tests still assert against the pre-lean-schema record shape. **Confirm this by bisecting** (`git log --oneline -- src/papyrus_content/reference_url_text.py` then check out each candidate and run the suite) rather than assuming.

## The decision this needs

For each failing test, determine which of these it is, and say so explicitly in the fix:

1. **Test is stale** — it asserts a record shape the lean schema intentionally changed. Update the expectation. Low risk.
2. **Test is correct and the code regressed** — the lean-schema change dropped something it should not have. Fix the code. This would be a real production bug in reference ingestion, so it matters which one it is.

Do not bulk-update assertions to make the suite green. That converts a possible real regression into a permanently hidden one, which is the same failure mode that let the `corpus_key` bug through.

## Acceptance criteria

- `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m pytest procedures/newsroom/tests/test_references_commands.py` is green.
- Each fixed test is categorised (stale expectation vs. real regression) in the commit message or a comment here.
- Any test found to be masking a genuine regression gets that regression fixed, not its assertion relaxed.

issues.description:
Deliberately allocate a fraction of automated research to territory adjacent to what the humans have explicitly steered toward, so the system can surface things nobody thought to ask for.

## Why this needs to be designed, not assumed

A core goal of Papyrus is to **surprise its operators with insights they did not consciously set out to find**. That property does not emerge from a well-tuned system — it has to be budgeted for, and most of our other work actively suppresses it.

Every mechanism we have sharpens focus: corpus scoping, category steering, per-desk defaults, coverage themes, and (proposed) named scope bundles all narrow research toward what is already tracked. Each is individually correct and collectively they converge on efficient coverage of known territory with zero discovery. Relevance ranking has the same bias: it rewards similarity to the query, and surprise is by definition not similar to what you asked.

This is the exploration/exploitation tradeoff, and right now the system is pure exploitation. Nothing on the board changes that; the scope-bundles epic makes it worse. So this is recorded as an explicit counterweight.

## The steering frame

The intended operating model is that humans **steer** rather than **operate**. Steering implies the vehicle covers ground the driver did not individually specify — otherwise it is operating with extra steps. An automated research loop that only ever fetches what it was pointed at is not steerable; it is remote-controlled.

## Design directions (nothing settled yet — this issue is partly a research question)

1. **An explicit exploration budget.** Some fraction of scheduled research dispatches — a fifth is a reasonable starting guess — targets adjacent rather than tracked territory. Making it a fraction of an existing budget rather than an unbounded extra keeps the cost story intact.
2. **Where "adjacent" comes from.** Several candidate sources, worth comparing rather than picking blind:
   - Ontology neighbors: concepts one or two hops from tracked `SemanticNode`s along `broader_than` / `narrower_than` / `mentions` edges that have low `acceptedReferenceMentionCount`. The graph already knows what is near-but-thin.
   - Coverage gaps already computed by the coverage-theme machinery.
   - Rejected-reference scope memory read *inversely*: repeatedly-rejected-adjacent topics are a boundary; topics rejected once for incidental reasons may be worth revisiting.
   - Sources cited BY accepted references but never themselves ingested — the citation graph already records these and they are pre-vetted by an author we already accepted.
3. **Surface exploration results differently from steered results.** If exploratory findings enter the same curation queue with the same framing, they will be rejected at a higher rate simply for being unfamiliar, and the mechanism will quietly die. They should arrive labeled as exploratory with the "why this might matter" rationale foregrounded.
4. **Measure whether it works.** The metric is not volume but **acceptance rate of exploratory prospects, and the eventual publication rate of what gets accepted**. If exploratory prospects are accepted at a decent clip, raise the budget. If they are near-universally rejected, either the adjacency signal is bad or the framing is bad — diagnose which before abandoning it.

## Dependencies and tensions

- Pulls against **named scope bundles**, which narrow defaults. Both can be right: bundles for steered work, an explicit exploration lane that ignores them.
- Benefits from **entity resolution + graph promotion**, which is what makes ontology-neighbor adjacency meaningful (a denser graph has more usable neighbors).
- Constrained by **curation throughput** — exploration adds review load, which is the actual bottleneck. Best paired with assisted triage; without it, this epic spends the scarcest resource in the system.

## What could go wrong

- **Noise floods the queue**, curation burns out, and the operator starts rubber-stamping — which damages the main curation path too. Bound the budget hard; start smaller than feels interesting.
- **"Adjacent" degenerates into "random."** Adjacency must be a real graph or citation signal, not a temperature knob on a search query.
- **Measured as volume rather than value.** More prospects is not the goal; more accepted surprises is.
- **Never actually built** because it is nobody's urgent problem — the most likely failure. It is the mechanism by which the publication stays interesting rather than merely current.
issues.title: Exploratory research budget: surface adjacent, unsteered territory

issues.description:
Feature-flagged small-LLM rerank over the fused top ~20 candidates, plus adjacent-chunk context expansion for winners. LAST in the roadmap on purpose: it is the only epic that adds a RECURRING per-query LLM cost, and the fused + decayed + distilled stack may make it unnecessary outside the chat profile.

BLOCKED BY: hybrid-lexical epic (rerank consumes the fused list; without hybrid recall it just polishes a biased pool).
GATED BY: the retrieval eval harness epic — that harness is now a separate, earlier epic and its golden set is the decision instrument here. Do not build the harness inside this epic.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-19)

- No rerank pass exists. Ranking is the weighted blend in `score_record` (`src/papyrus_knowledge_query/ranking.py:236-266`).
- The query engine is currently LLM-free — the only external call is the OpenAI EMBEDDING request (`services.py:382-395` region). Adding a completion call is a new class of latency and failure inside the Lambda. The 300s timeout is ample; user-perceived latency (+1–3s) is the real cost.
- Context-expansion machinery mostly exists: chunk metadata carries `chunkIndex`/`startChar`/`endChar` (`vector_index.py:748-751`), and the evidence path already re-reads source text (`_collect_reference_evidence` / `_seed_evidence_from_semantic_passages`, `engine.py:1727+` region).
- Agent-side reranking already happens implicitly: `research_explorer.tac` reads evidence and chooses. That is the alternative that makes this epic optional.

## Design decisions (current thinking — challenge them if you have better information)

1. **Context expansion lands FIRST and independently of the rerank verdict.** For top evidence chunks, stitch `chunkIndex ± 1` neighbors from extracted text via the corpus text provider before evidence packing, capped by existing token budgets. No LLM, cheap, and it fixes orphaned-fragment snippets regardless of whether reranking ever ships. Dedupe by chunk key (reuse `_dedupe_passages`) — adjacent chunks may already be selected.
2. **`src/papyrus_knowledge_query/reranker.py`**: one batched completion call scoring the fused top 20 (per candidate: title + summary/chunk text, ≤300 chars) against the query, returning 0–10 integer scores as strict JSON. Keep top 10. Model from env `PAPYRUS_RERANK_MODEL`; do not hardcode a vendor-dated model name.
3. **Flag**: `ranking.rerank: true`, default FALSE everywhere. No profile opts in as part of this epic.
4. **Failure containment**: 5s client timeout, one retry on malformed JSON, then FALL BACK to fused order with a warning. A rerank failure must never fail the query.
5. **Score integration**: write `ranking.rerankScore`; fold into relevance only when the flag is on. Preserve `fusion.{semanticRank, lexicalRank, rrfScore}` provenance so the eval can compare orderings.
6. **Prompt-injection hardening**: candidate titles and snippets are untrusted corpus text going into a completion prompt. The prompt must treat them strictly as data to be scored, never as instructions. Cheap to include, do not skip.
7. **The eval decides.** Run the golden set with rerank off vs on, temperature 0, 3 runs, report variance and per-category deltas. Orderings that flip between identical runs are themselves evidence against shipping.

## Decision rule (state the outcome explicitly in this epic before closing)

- Clear per-category win that justifies +1–3s and per-query cost → ship, still default-off, opt in for the chat profile only.
- No clear win → **close as not-shipped. That is a SUCCESS outcome, not a failure.** We keep the context expansion, we keep the eval numbers, and we have bought certainty that we are not paying a recurring LLM tax for nothing. Record the numbers in this epic so nobody re-proposes it from intuition later.

## Files to modify

- NEW `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/reranker.py`
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/engine.py` — flag handling between fusion and normalization; adjacent-chunk stitching in the evidence path
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/ranking.py` — `normalize_ranking_config` accepts `rerank` bool
- Tests: fallback-on-timeout, malformed-JSON-retry, flag-off-is-byte-identical, stitching respects token budget, injection-resistant prompt shape

## What could go wrong

- **Cost creep**: if any default profile silently opts in, every newsroom procedure query pays the rerank tax. The flag-off-byte-identical test is the guard; grep for `rerank` in procedure configs at review time.
- **Nondeterminism** masquerading as improvement — see decision 7.
- **Motivated reasoning**: whoever builds the reranker will want it to win. The eval baseline was captured before this epic existed, which is the protection; do not adjust the golden set during this epic.

## Out of scope

Building the eval harness (separate earlier epic), turning rerank on for any profile (separate decision after eval), self-hosted rerank models (nothing self-hosted — scale-to-zero), reranking inside MCP primitive tools (agents orchestrate their own).
issues.title: Feature-flagged LLM rerank + context expansion (eval-gated)
